Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
Being alone in a room or building
hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: When Julian was twenty, a ruptured gas line in his parents' basement workshop engulfed his older brother in flames. He arrived to find the heavy steel door jammed shut, the heat still radiating through the metal. From that day, the scent of scorched rubber became an immediate trigger, dragging the event into his mind as a series of vivid, unchanging photographs. Because he could not put the horror into words, the memories arrived as silent, graphic frames that bypassed language entirely. The smell alone would spike his physiological alarm, throwing him into a state of hypervigilance where every sudden movement near him put him instantly on guard. He found himself scanning doorways for people acting suspiciously, his nervous system treating ordinary glances as imminent danger. This constant state of alarm soon dictated his coping habits; as soon as the photographic memories or a family member's well-meaning comment about his brother surfaced in their shared kitchen, Julian would immediately switch off the television, refuse to read any news, and retreat to the garage where Clara had to sit beside him. He could not bear the quiet of an empty hallway, and when the emotional pressure became unmanageable, he would pinch his forearm until the sharp pain grounded him. Over the following months, these patterns calcified into a rigid routine that tightened his distress within their cramped apartment. The trigger of a suspicious glance directly funneled into his need to avoid media and solitude, while the trigger of a sudden movement directly spiked his physiological threat. The trigger of a family comment directly pulled the event into his mind as silent, photographic frames. Because the intrusive memories refused to fade, they directly pushed him toward switching off the television and demanding Clara's presence. His exhaustion from sleeplessness and the relentless flashbacks directly increased his reliance on self-inflicted pain to release overwhelming feelings. As his body kept reacting as if he were still trapped in the burning basement, Julian began to view his own physiology as an enemy that betrayed him the moment he was safe. The unresolved threat only deepened his negative appraisals that he was no longer capable of managing his own life and could not rely on himself. The persistence of these silent frames directly deepened his conviction that he had lost his competence. Unable to trust his own reactions, his negative appraisals directly heightened his scanning for suspicious people before allowing himself to relax. His deepening negative appraisals made ordinary family comments feel like unbearable indictments, which in turn trained him to perceive threat in ordinary movements. Each time he numbbed his panic with a sharp pain, his refusal to stay alone directly ensured he would continue to perceive ordinary glances as suspicious. His reliance on self-harm directly kept his threat system primed, while his avoidance of media prevented his brain from integrating the photographic memories, ensuring they remained vivid. By the time Julian finally sought help, he was twenty-one and unemployed, his job applications abandoned after he stopped leaving the house. He came to the clinic because Clara had left him to stay with her sister for three days, and the sudden silence had triggered a panic so severe he had cut his own wrist to survive it. He was terrified of relapsing into that isolation, yet he desperately hoped to stop feeling like a stranger in his own skin. What he most wanted was to trust his own mind again, to walk into a room without bracing for the worst, and to finally speak his brother's story without it fracturing into silent, burning photographs.
